Why Is It Called Godzilla Minus Zero?

  • Chris Lambert
  • November 3, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:38
Instaread

Believe it or not, the title Godzilla Minus Zero is actually a positive one. Let me explain.

The “Godzilla minus” title meaning

The original title for this version of Godzilla was a reference to Japan after the war. Writer-director Takashi Yamazaki explained that Japan was at “zero” after World War II. He showed this by focusing on those attempting to live in the wake of the bombing of Tokyo. Then Godzilla shows up. And Godzilla is another deduction. If you’re already at zero, then the next number back is negative one. 

So the title Godzilla Minus Zero implies not just the next installment in the series but a sense of forward progress for the characters.

Takashi Yamazaki said in an interview: In certain disciplines of math, there is…sometimes a minus in front of the zero, and I think the meaning is that you are approaching, it’s like approaching [the] limit, approaching this number, zero. And, for me, that was what I was thinking of when making this film.

I think it’s going to have many meanings, but this family, this Shikishima family, is…approaching this limit of zero, like going back to neutral in a lot of ways. And, for me, I think that feeling is captured in the “Godzilla Minus Zero” because they’re not quite there. They’re still in the process of approaching it. 

For me, this idea of getting back to zero clarified the character arcs for Shikishima, Noriko, and Akiko. In Minus One, everyone struggled with grief. But in Minus Zero, there’s a renewed sense of moving forward and letting the past be the past. It isn’t just the monsters that evolve and grow stronger. People do, too. 

Yamazaki’s first Godzilla film was about a step in the negative direction, while the sequel is about a return to neutral. That sets up a continued progression into the positive. The obvious title for the third film is Godzilla Plus One. We’ll see if that’s what happens or if Yamazaki feels the need to subvert both expectations and his established naming conventions.
